questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: A chemical processing industry uses a water-tube boiler that generates 22% wet steam at 900 kPa. The hourly steam requirement is 780 kg and the feed water is at 28°C. The boiler is fired with wood pellets and coconut shell in a 6:4 mass ratio, with gross calorific values 19600 kJ/kg and 20800 kJ/kg respectively. The boiler efficiency is 60%. Calculate the hourly consumption of wood pellets and coconut shells. To improve efficiency, two options are considered, both reducing fuel consumption by 12%: (i) an economizer that raises the feed water temperature by 50°C, and (ii) an air preheater that improves combustion. Compare the resulting boiler efficiencies and recommend an option.
questions.solution: At 0.9 MPa, hf = 742.6 kJ/kg and hfg = 2030.5 kJ/kg, so h = 742.6 + 0.78 × 2030.5 = 2326.4 kJ/kg. Feed enthalpy = 4.186 × 28 = 117.2 kJ/kg. Heat required = 780 × (2326.4 - 117.2) = 1.723×10^6 kJ/h. Fuel energy input = 1.723×10^6/0.60 = 2.872×10^6 kJ/h. Mixture GCV = 0.6 × 19600 + 0.4 × 20800 = 20080 kJ/kg, so fuel rate = 2.872×10^6/20080 = 143 kg/h: wood = 85.8 kg/h, coconut shell = 57.2 kg/h. (i) Economizer: heat required becomes 780 × (2326.4 - 117.2 - 209.3) = 1.560×10^6 kJ/h; fuel input falls 12% to 2.527×10^6 kJ/h, giving η = 1.560/2.527 = 61.7%. (ii) Air preheater: heat required stays 1.723×10^6 kJ/h; fuel input is again 2.527×10^6 kJ/h, giving η = 68.2%. The air preheater gives the higher efficiency, so it should be selected.
questions.note: Steam-table values at 0.9 MPa are used; small differences in table data change the last digit only.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: 1310 kg of steam that is 15.75% wet is produced in a boiler at 2.5 N/mm². The steam enters a superheater where its temperature is raised until the degree of superheat is 160°C. From the superheater the steam passes through a heat exchanger for process heating, where it loses 27.2% of its enthalpy. If the feed water temperature is 32°C, determine (i) the total heat added to the feed water in the boiler, (ii) the total heat supplied in the superheater and (iii) the condition and related parameter of the steam at the exit of the heat exchanger.
questions.solution: At 2.5 MPa: hf = 962.1 kJ/kg, hfg = 1839.4 kJ/kg, hg = 2801.5 kJ/kg, Tsat = 223.9°C. Wet steam: h1 = 962.1 + 0.8425 × 1839.4 = 2511.8 kJ/kg. Feed enthalpy = 4.186 × 32 = 134.0 kJ/kg. (i) Boiler heat = 1310 × (2511.8 - 134.0) = 3.115×10^6 kJ. (ii) Superheated steam: h2 = 2801.5 + 2.25 × 160 = 3161.5 kJ/kg. Superheater heat = 1310 × (3161.5 - 2511.8) = 8.51×10^5 kJ. (iii) After losing 27.2% of enthalpy, h3 = 0.728 × 3161.5 = 2301.6 kJ/kg. Since hf < h3 < hg, the steam is wet: x = (2301.6 - 962.1)/1839.4 = 0.728. The exit steam is 27.2% wet (dryness fraction 0.728).

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Give reasons for the following: (i) Boiler mountings are an integral part of a boiler. (ii) Saturated steam cannot be produced in the boiler drum. (iii) Water-tube boilers generally operate at higher pressures.
questions.solution: (i) Mountings such as safety valves, pressure gauges, water-level indicators and feed-water valves are essential for safe operation and are mounted directly on the boiler shell. (ii) Steam generated in the drum is in contact with water and carries moisture; it becomes dry saturated only after passing through a separator/superheater, so the drum produces wet steam rather than strictly dry saturated steam. (iii) In a water-tube boiler the water circulates inside small-diameter tubes, which can be made strong enough to withstand high pressure, while the surrounding shell is not subjected to the full pressure.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: A boiler supplies steam at 3 N/mm² and 300°C at 5000 kg/hr. Feed water is supplied at 30°C and fuel at 800 kg/hr with calorific value 22 MJ/kg. (i) Find the boiler efficiency. (ii) If the efficiency is to be increased by 5% in absolute terms, what should be the ratio of steam generation rate to fuel consumption rate, assuming the heat gained by water remains the same? (iii) If an economizer preheats the feed water by 5°C and reduces fuel consumption by 5%, what is the new efficiency? Take cp(water) = 4.18 kJ/kg K and cp(superheated steam) = 2.25 kJ/kg K.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: 5 kg of steam at 2 bar is supplied to a pipeline at 200°C. Due to poor insulation, the steam loses 2000 kJ of heat in the pipeline at constant pressure. The steam leaving the pipeline is supplied to a turbine, where it must be superheated with a degree of superheat of 100°C. What quantity of heat must be supplied at the pipeline exit to reach the required turbine-inlet condition? Take cp(superheated steam) = 2.25 kJ/kg K.
questions.solution: At 2 bar, Tsat = 120.2°C and hg = 2706.3 kJ/kg. Initial h = 2706.3 + 2.25 × (200 - 120.2) = 2885.9 kJ/kg. After losing 2000 kJ for 5 kg, h = 2885.9 - 400 = 2485.9 kJ/kg. Since hf = 504.7 and hfg = 2201.9 kJ/kg, the steam is wet with x = (2485.9 - 504.7)/2201.9 = 0.900. The required turbine-inlet state has 100°C superheat: h_req = 2706.3 + 2.25 × 100 = 2931.3 kJ/kg. Heat to be supplied = 5 × (2931.3 - 2485.9) = 2227 kJ.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Explain any three differences between a boiler mounting and a boiler accessory.
questions.solution: 1. Mountings are essential for the safe operation of the boiler, whereas accessories are used to improve efficiency or performance and are not essential for safety. 2. Mountings are mounted directly on the boiler shell (safety valve, pressure gauge, water-level indicator), while accessories are separate auxiliary equipment (economizer, air preheater, superheater). 3. Failure of a mounting can be dangerous and may stop the boiler, whereas failure of an accessory usually reduces efficiency but does not directly endanger the boiler.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Equal quantities of steam are supplied to a mixing chamber from two boilers. One supplies steam that is 9% wet and the other supplies superheated steam at 308°C. The pressure in both boilers and in the mixing chamber is 15 bar. Determine the quality and temperature of the steam in the mixing chamber. Take cp(superheated steam) = 2.25 kJ/kg K.
questions.solution: At 15 bar: hf = 844.7 kJ/kg, hfg = 1945.3 kJ/kg, hg = 2790.0 kJ/kg, Tsat = 198.3°C. Wet steam: h1 = 844.7 + 0.91 × 1945.3 = 2614.9 kJ/kg. Superheated steam: h2 = 2790.0 + 2.25 × (308 - 198.3) = 3036.8 kJ/kg. For equal masses, h_mix = (h1 + h2)/2 = 2825.9 kJ/kg. This is above hg, so the mixture is superheated. Its temperature is T = 198.3 + (2825.9 - 2790.0)/2.25 = 214.3°C, i.e. about 16°C of superheat.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Draw a neat sketch of a water-tube boiler, indicate the path of the flue gases and name the parts.
questions.solution: A typical water-tube boiler has a mud drum at the bottom and a steam drum at the top, connected by inclined water tubes that form the furnace walls. Fuel burns in the furnace and hot flue gases rise around the tubes, transferring heat to the water inside, then pass through the superheater, economizer and air preheater before leaving through the chimney. Water circulates from the mud drum through the tubes to the steam drum, where steam separates. Key parts: furnace, water tubes, steam drum, mud drum, superheater, economizer, air preheater, grate and chimney.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Define: (a) dry saturated steam, (b) superheated steam, (c) critical point and (d) latent heat of evaporation.
questions.solution: (a) Dry saturated steam is steam at the saturation temperature for its pressure, containing no suspended moisture (dryness fraction x = 1). (b) Superheated steam is steam heated above its saturation temperature at the same pressure; the difference between its temperature and the saturation temperature is the degree of superheat. (c) The critical point is the state at which the liquid and vapour phases are indistinguishable, for water at about 374°C and 221.2 bar. (d) Latent heat of evaporation is the heat required to convert 1 kg of saturated liquid into dry saturated vapour at constant pressure and temperature.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Explain the formation of steam at constant pressure with a temperature-enthalpy diagram.
questions.solution: At constant pressure, water is heated from its initial temperature to the saturation temperature (sensible heating), absorbing hf. Further heat at constant temperature evaporates the water into wet steam, absorbing the latent heat xhfg; at x = 1 the steam is dry saturated. Additional heating produces superheated steam, whose temperature rises above saturation and whose enthalpy is hg + cp(T - Tsat). On a T-h diagram this appears as a rising liquid line, a horizontal evaporation line inside the dome, and a rising superheat line outside the dome. The saturation curve ends at the critical point.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Define and write expressions for (i) enthalpy of dry saturated steam, (ii) enthalpy of wet steam and (iii) enthalpy of superheated steam.
questions.solution: (i) Dry saturated steam: hg = hf + hfg, where hf is the sensible heat of saturated liquid and hfg is the latent heat at the given pressure. (ii) Wet steam with dryness fraction x: h = hf + xhfg. (iii) Superheated steam: h = hg + cp(T_sup - Tsat) = hf + hfg + cp(T_sup - Tsat), where cp is the specific heat of superheated steam.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Determine the condition of steam in the following cases: (i) at 10 bar and 200°C, (ii) at 8 bar with enthalpy 2500 kJ/kg, (iii) steam at 20 bar and 300°C is cooled at constant pressure while losing 400 kJ/kg.
questions.solution: (i) At 10 bar, Tsat = 179.9°C. Since 200°C > Tsat, the steam is superheated by 20.1°C. (ii) At 8 bar, hf = 721.1, hfg = 2048.0 and hg = 2769.1 kJ/kg. Since 2500 < hg, the steam is wet: x = (2500 - 721.1)/2048.0 = 0.868, i.e. 13.2% wet. (iii) At 20 bar, Tsat = 212.4°C and hg = 2799.5 kJ/kg; initially h = 2799.5 + 2.25 × (300 - 212.4) = 2996.6 kJ/kg. After losing 400 kJ/kg, h = 2596.6 kJ/kg. With hf = 908.8 and hfg = 1890.7 kJ/kg, x = (2596.6 - 908.8)/1890.7 = 0.893, so the steam is 10.7% wet.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: With respect to the Babcock and Wilcox boiler, give a brief description of (i) the function of the chain-grate stoker, (ii) the water circuit in the boiler and (iii) superheating of the steam.
questions.solution: (i) The chain-grate stoker is an endless moving grate that carries coal slowly through the furnace, so fresh coal is heated, ignited and burned progressively; it gives uniform combustion and automatic ash removal. (ii) Feed water enters the steam drum, flows down the rear header through the inclined water tubes to the front header, and returns to the drum. Heating in the tubes sets up natural circulation, and steam separates in the drum. (iii) Saturated steam from the drum passes through a superheater placed in the flue-gas path, where it is heated above saturation temperature; this raises the steam temperature and improves cycle efficiency while reducing condensation in the turbine.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Draw a neat sketch of a locomotive boiler and explain it briefly.
questions.solution: A locomotive boiler is a horizontal fire-tube boiler with a cylindrical shell, a firebox at the rear and a smoke box at the front. Hot gases from the firebox pass through fire tubes to the smoke box and out through the chimney, heating the surrounding water. A steam dome collects steam, and a superheater in the tubes raises its temperature. The boiler is compact and has a large grate area, making it suitable for locomotives; it is externally fired and uses a brick arch to improve combustion.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Steam enters a superheater with an initial condition of 12 bar and 13% wet. Its temperature is raised in the superheater until the degree of superheat is 205°C. If the feed water temperature is 24°C, determine (i) the total heat added to the feed water in the boiler and (ii) the amount of superheat. Give the answer per kg of steam.
questions.solution: At 12 bar: hf = 798.6, hfg = 1986.2, hg = 2784.8 kJ/kg, Tsat = 188.0°C. Wet steam: h1 = 798.6 + 0.87 × 1986.2 = 2526.6 kJ/kg. Feed enthalpy = 4.186 × 24 = 100.5 kJ/kg. (i) Boiler heat = h1 - h_feed = 2526.6 - 100.5 = 2426.1 kJ/kg. (ii) Superheated steam: h2 = 2784.8 + 2.25 × 205 = 3246.1 kJ/kg. Superheat added = h2 - h1 = 719.5 kJ/kg.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Define the following and write expressions where applicable: (i) sensible heat, (ii) degree of superheat and (iii) latent heat of evaporation.
questions.solution: (i) Sensible heat is the heat added to raise the temperature of 1 kg of water from a reference temperature (usually 0°C) to its saturation temperature: hf = cp(Tsat - 0). (ii) Degree of superheat is the difference between the temperature of superheated steam and the saturation temperature at the same pressure: ΔT = T_sup - Tsat. (iii) Latent heat of evaporation hfg is the heat required to convert 1 kg of saturated liquid into dry saturated vapour at constant pressure and temperature.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: A crusher in a mining setup uses a flat belt drive to transmit power between two parallel shafts running in opposite directions. The driver pulley has a diameter of 300 mm and the output shaft rotates at 250 rpm. The centre distance is 800 mm and the speed reduction ratio is 3/2. Given an initial tension of 1500 N in the belt, determine the tensions on the tight and slack sides, the power transmitted and the length of the belt. Take the coefficient of friction as 0.28.
questions.solution: Speed reduction 3/2 means N1/N2 = 3/2, so N1 = 375 rpm and D2 = 1.5 × 0.30 = 0.45 m. Belt speed v = πD1N1/60 = π × 0.30 × 375/60 = 5.89 m/s. For an open belt, sinα = (D2 - D1)/(2C) = 0.15/1.6 = 0.09375, so α = 5.38° = 0.0939 rad and the contact angle on the smaller pulley is θ = π - 2α = 2.954 rad. Then T1/T2 = e^(μθ) = e^(0.28 × 2.954) = 2.29. With T1 + T2 = 2 × 1500 = 3000 N, T1 = 2087 N and T2 = 913 N. Power = (T1 - T2)v = 1174 × 5.89 ≈ 6.9 kW. Belt length = 2C + π(D1 + D2)/2 + (D2 - D1)²/(4C) = 1.6 + 1.178 + 0.007 = 2.79 m.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: An electric bike uses a flat open belt drive between the motor shaft and the wheel shaft, with a centre distance of 500 mm. The velocity ratio is limited to 3. The maximum tension in the belt is 1740 N. The speed and diameter of the driver pulley are 300 rpm and 100 mm. What power is transmitted and what is the length of the belt? Take μ = 0.3.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: List any three advantages of a belt drive system and any three advantages of a chain drive system.
questions.solution: Belt drive: (1) simple and cheap, with no lubrication needed; (2) absorbs shock and vibration and protects the machine from overload by slipping; (3) can transmit power over long centre distances and is quiet. Chain drive: (1) positive drive with no slip, giving an exact velocity ratio; (2) compact and capable of transmitting high torque; (3) suitable for high temperatures and dirty environments, with higher efficiency than a belt.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Sketch and explain the arrangement of a fast and loose pulley.
questions.solution: Two pulleys of the same diameter are mounted side by side on the driven shaft: the fast pulley is keyed to the shaft and rotates with it, while the loose pulley turns freely on the shaft. An open belt runs over both. To drive the machine, the belt is shifted onto the fast pulley, usually by a fork; to stop it, the belt is shifted onto the loose pulley, which spins idly while the shaft remains stationary. This provides a simple clutch for starting and stopping without stopping the prime mover.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: A belt drive transmitting power between two pulleys 2 m apart has a speed reduction ratio of 4 and an angle of contact of 3.91 rad. The diameter of the larger pulley is 120 cm and the driver pulley runs at 1600 rpm. The initial tension in the belt is 0.95 kN and the coefficient of friction is 0.28. Calculate the length of the belt, the power transmitted and the width of the belt if the permissible tension per metre width is 10 kN.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Explain with sketches: (i) speed cone and (ii) fast and loose pulley.
questions.solution: (i) A speed cone (stepped pulley) consists of a cone with several steps of different diameters, paired with an identical cone on the driven shaft and connected by a belt. Moving the belt from one step to another changes the diameter ratio and hence the output speed, giving a range of discrete speeds. (ii) The fast pulley is keyed to the shaft and drives it; the loose pulley rotates freely on the same shaft. Shifting the belt from the fast to the loose pulley stops the driven shaft while the prime mover keeps running.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: A machine is driven by a motor at 1200 rpm through a belt drive with a speed reduction ratio of 4, followed by a compound gear train with six spur gears A, B, C, D, E and F. A meshes with B, C with D and E with F; B and C are on one shaft, and D and E on another. Gear A has 30 teeth with module 3 mm, gear D has module 2 mm and 126 teeth, and gear E has module 2 mm and 24 teeth. The speed reductions are A to B = 2, C to D = 3 and E to F = 5. Find the teeth numbers of B, C and F, the speed of gear F and the centre distances of the gear train. Show the arrangement.
questions.solution: B = 2 × 30 = 60 teeth. C to D reduction 3 means D = 3C, so C = 126/3 = 42 teeth. F = 5 × 24 = 120 teeth. The belt reduces the motor speed by 4, so gear A runs at 1200/4 = 300 rpm. The gear train reduction is 2 × 3 × 5 = 30, so N_F = 300/30 = 10 rpm. Centre distances: A-B = (30 + 60) × 3/2 = 135 mm; C-D = (42 + 126) × 2/2 = 168 mm; E-F = (24 + 120) × 2/2 = 144 mm. Arrangement: motor → belt → A on shaft 1, B and C on shaft 2, D and E on shaft 3, F on shaft 4.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: A set of gear wheels is available to form a compound gear train. Sketch an arrangement using four shafts that gives the maximum velocity ratio, calculate the ratio if the largest-to-smallest tooth ratio at each stage is used, and state the conditions for achieving maximum velocity ratio.
questions.solution: Mount the smallest gear as the driver on the first shaft and the largest gear as the driven gear on the second shaft; on the second shaft mount the smallest remaining gear, driving the largest remaining gear on the third shaft, and repeat for the fourth shaft. The overall ratio is the product of the individual tooth ratios. To maximise it: (1) use a compound rather than a simple train, (2) at every stage use the largest possible driven gear with the smallest possible driver, (3) keep each pair on separate shafts and ensure meshing gears have the same module, and (4) avoid interference and keep the centre distances practical.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: A gear train consists of four gears A, B, C and D with 20, 40, 80 and 100 teeth respectively. Show the arrangement of the gears for a maximum speed reduction of 2.5.
questions.solution: To use all four gears and obtain exactly 2.5, make a compound train in which the first stage reduces speed and the second stage increases it. Let gear A (20 teeth) drive gear D (100 teeth), giving a reduction of 100/20 = 5. Mount gear C (80 teeth) on the same shaft as D, and let C drive gear B (40 teeth), giving a speed increase of 40/80 = 0.5. The overall ratio is 5 × 0.5 = 2.5. Thus A meshes with D, while C meshes with B; B and C are not on the same shaft.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: A compound gear train consists of four gear wheels A, B, C and D. A is the driver with 40 teeth and meshes with B. Gears B and C are mounted on the same shaft. C has 32 teeth and meshes with D. The speed is reduced from A to D by 93.75%. The speed reduction from A to B is the same as that from C to D. Determine the number of teeth on B and D and sketch the arrangement.
questions.solution: A reduction of 93.75% means N_D/N_A = 1 - 0.9375 = 0.0625 = 1/16. For a compound train, N_D/N_A = (T_A/T_B)(T_C/T_D) = r², where r is the common stage ratio. Thus r² = 1/16 and r = 1/4. Hence T_B = 4T_A = 160 teeth and T_D = 4T_C = 128 teeth. Arrangement: A (40) on the input shaft meshes with B (160); B and C (32) are keyed on the intermediate shaft; C meshes with D (128) on the output shaft.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: The following data refer to a twin-cylinder IC engine: cylinder diameter 200 mm, stroke 300 mm, total revolutions 18000 per hour, mean effective pressure 6 bar, fuel consumption 15 litres/hour, calorific value 45000 kJ/kg and specific gravity of fuel 0.8. Determine the indicated thermal efficiency.
questions.solution: For a two-stroke engine, N = 18000/60 = 300 rpm and the number of working strokes per minute equals the speed. Area = π(0.2)²/4 = 0.0314 m². IP = p_m L A N n/60 with n = 2 cylinders: IP = 6×10^5 × 0.3 × 0.0314 × 300 × 2/60 = 56.5 kW. Fuel mass flow = 15 × 0.8 = 12 kg/h, so fuel power = 12 × 45000/3600 = 150 kW. Indicated thermal efficiency = 56.5/150 = 37.7%. For a four-stroke engine the indicated power would be half this value, giving about 18.9%.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Sketch and explain the working principle of an IC engine fitted with a carburettor and a camshaft.
questions.solution: In a spark-ignition engine, air flows through the carburettor venturi; the reduced pressure draws petrol through a jet, and the air-fuel mixture enters the cylinder through the inlet valve. The camshaft carries cams that open the inlet and exhaust valves at the correct times and, in older engines, drives the ignition distributor. The piston moves down on the intake stroke, is compressed and ignited by the spark plug, and the burnt gases are pushed out on the exhaust stroke; the camshaft is driven at half the crankshaft speed in a four-stroke engine.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Give reasons for the following: (i) Four-stroke engines are more fuel efficient than two-stroke engines. (ii) A petrol engine is lighter than a diesel engine. (iii) A high rate of wear and tear occurs in two-stroke engines.
questions.solution: (i) In a four-stroke engine the exhaust and intake strokes are separate, so scavenging losses are small and combustion is more complete; a two-stroke engine loses fresh charge through the exhaust ports. (ii) A petrol engine operates at a lower compression ratio and peak pressure, so its cylinder, piston and connecting rod can be lighter; a diesel engine needs heavier components to withstand high compression and pressure. (iii) A two-stroke engine fires every revolution, so it runs hotter and has twice as many power strokes; lubrication is often mixed with the fuel and port scavenging washes oil away, increasing wear.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: A twin-cylinder diesel engine admits charge into the cylinder indirectly and has a fuel consumption of 0.257 kg/kWh at 25 cycles per second. The calorific value of diesel is 43900 kJ/kg. The net brake load is 70 kg and the mean circumference of the brake drum is 4 m. Determine the brake thermal efficiency.
questions.solution: Brake torque T = W × R, where R = circumference/(2π) = 4/(2π) = 0.6366 m. Thus T = 70 × 9.81 × 0.6366 = 437.1 N m. With N = 25 rev/s = 1500 rpm, BP = 2πNT/60 = 2π × 1500 × 437.1/60 = 68.7 kW. Fuel consumption = 0.257 × 68.7 = 17.65 kg/h, so fuel power = 17.65 × 43900/3600 = 215.2 kW. Brake thermal efficiency = 68.7/215.2 = 31.9%.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Identify and explain the working of an IC engine that admits the charge indirectly and has a compression ratio of 9.
questions.solution: An engine with indirect charge admission (through a carburettor or port injection) and a compression ratio of about 9 is a four-stroke spark-ignition (petrol) engine. During the intake stroke the air-fuel mixture is drawn in; the mixture is compressed on the compression stroke and ignited by a spark near top dead centre. The hot gases expand on the power stroke, doing work on the piston, and are expelled on the exhaust stroke. A compression ratio of 9 is typical for petrol engines, limited by knock.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Justify the following statements: (i) Brake power cannot be equal to or greater than indicated power. (ii) Two-stroke engines do not need a camshaft. (iii) A heavier flywheel is used in four-stroke engines.
questions.solution: (i) Brake power is the power available at the shaft after friction and pumping losses, so BP = IP - FP; friction power is always positive, hence BP < IP. (ii) In a two-stroke engine the piston itself uncovers the inlet, transfer and exhaust ports as it moves, so valve actuation by a camshaft is unnecessary. (iii) A four-stroke engine produces one power stroke every two revolutions, so the torque pulses are more widely spaced; a heavier flywheel is needed to store energy and keep the speed uniform. A two-stroke engine fires every revolution and needs less flywheel mass.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Mention any four differences between a four-stroke engine and a two-stroke engine, and with a neat diagram explain the working of a simple carburettor.
questions.solution: Differences: (1) A four-stroke engine has four piston strokes per power stroke; a two-stroke has two. (2) The four-stroke uses valves; the two-stroke usually uses ports uncovered by the piston. (3) A four-stroke fires once every two revolutions; a two-stroke fires every revolution. (4) A four-stroke has separate intake and exhaust strokes and better scavenging, while a two-stroke loses some fresh charge through the exhaust. Carburettor: air enters through a venturi; the pressure drop draws fuel through a jet, atomizing it into the air stream. A throttle valve controls the mixture flow, and a float chamber maintains a constant fuel level. The resulting air-fuel mixture enters the engine cylinder.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Explain the splash lubrication system used in IC engines with a neat sketch.
questions.solution: In splash lubrication, the crankcase contains an oil sump. A scoop or dipper on the big end of the connecting rod dips into the oil as the crankshaft rotates and splashes oil onto the cylinder walls, piston pin, bearings and camshaft. Oil holes and grooves distribute the oil to moving parts, and it drains back to the sump. The system is simple and cheap but less reliable at high speeds and for engines with many cylinders; a splash guard prevents excessive oil throwing.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Describe the working of a simple carburettor with a neat labelled sketch.
questions.solution: A simple carburettor consists of a float chamber, a fuel jet, a venturi, a throttle valve and a choke. Air enters through the venturi, where its velocity increases and pressure falls. The pressure difference between the float chamber and the venturi draws fuel through the jet, where it is atomized and mixed with the air. The float and needle valve maintain a constant fuel level. The throttle controls the quantity of mixture entering the engine, and the choke enriches the mixture during cold starting.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: List any ten comparisons between two-stroke and four-stroke engines.
questions.solution: 1. Strokes per cycle: two versus four. 2. Power strokes: every revolution versus every two revolutions. 3. Valves: ports versus inlet/exhaust valves. 4. Camshaft: not required versus required. 5. Flywheel: lighter versus heavier. 6. Scavenging: less efficient, some charge loss versus more efficient. 7. Fuel efficiency: lower versus higher. 8. Cooling: hotter running and harder to cool versus cooler. 9. Lubrication: often oil mixed with fuel versus separate lubricating system. 10. Applications: small two-wheelers, chainsaws and marine outboards versus cars, trucks and generators. Also, two-stroke engines have fewer moving parts and lower cost but higher emissions.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Discuss the working of a four-stroke diesel engine with the help of the theoretical Diesel cycle.
questions.solution: A four-stroke diesel engine has intake, compression, power and exhaust strokes. On intake, only air is drawn in. The air is compressed to a high ratio (typically 16-22), raising its temperature above the fuel's ignition point. Fuel is injected near the end of compression and burns at approximately constant pressure, pushing the piston down on the power stroke. The exhaust valve then releases the burnt gases. On a p-V diagram the Diesel cycle consists of isentropic compression, constant-pressure heat addition, isentropic expansion and constant-volume heat rejection. Its efficiency is η = 1 - (1/r^(γ-1))[(ρ^γ - 1)/(γ(ρ - 1))], where r is the compression ratio and ρ the cut-off ratio.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Explain the working principle of a CI engine.
questions.solution: A compression-ignition (diesel) engine draws only air into the cylinder on the intake stroke. The air is compressed to a high ratio, so its temperature rises above the fuel's auto-ignition temperature. Diesel is injected directly into the hot, high-pressure air near the end of compression, where it ignites spontaneously. The burning gases expand and drive the piston on the power stroke, and the exhaust stroke removes the burnt gases. A fuel pump and injector replace the spark plug, and the engine operates on the Diesel cycle with constant-pressure heat addition.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: With neat sketches, explain any four lathe operations.
questions.solution: 1. Turning: removes metal from the outside diameter of a rotating workpiece with a single-point tool fed along the axis. 2. Facing: feeds the tool radially across the end of the workpiece to produce a flat surface. 3. Chamfering: cuts an angled edge at the end of a shaft to remove sharp corners. 4. Knurling: presses a knurling tool into the rotating surface to form a serrated grip. Other common operations are drilling, boring, threading, grooving, parting and taper turning.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: With a neat sketch and labelling, explain the features of a radial drilling machine.
questions.solution: A radial drilling machine has a heavy base, a vertical column, a radial arm that can rotate and slide up or down on the column, and a drill head that slides along the arm. The spindle is mounted in the drill head and can be positioned anywhere over the workpiece by combining arm rotation, arm height and head travel. This makes it suitable for drilling large or heavy workpieces that cannot be moved easily. The spindle speed and feed are selected through the gearbox.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Identify and explain the lathe operations used for (i) removal of sharp corners on shaft ends and (ii) producing a serrated surface that helps in effective gripping.
questions.solution: (i) Removal of sharp corners on shaft ends is done by chamfering. The compound rest or tool post is set at an angle (usually 45°) and the tool is fed to cut a conical edge, which also helps guide mating parts and prevents injury. (ii) A serrated gripping surface is produced by knurling. A knurling tool holding hardened rollers with a diamond or straight pattern is pressed against the rotating workpiece, plastically deforming the surface into the required pattern. Knurling is used on handles, gauges and tool grips.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Compare reaming and boring with the help of neat sketches.
questions.solution: Boring enlarges an existing hole with a single-point boring tool on a lathe or boring machine. It can correct the hole's diameter, straightness and location, but removes more material and may leave tool marks. Reaming is a finishing operation that slightly enlarges a drilled hole and improves its dimensional accuracy and surface finish using a multi-edge reamer. Reaming removes very little material and cannot correct the position of a badly located hole. Boring is used before reaming when a large size change is needed.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Sketch and explain taper turning by the swivelling compound tool rest method.
questions.solution: The workpiece is held in the chuck and the compound rest is swivelled to half the included angle of the taper, α, where tanα = (D - d)/(2L). The tool is set at the required depth and fed manually along the swivelled slide while the workpiece rotates. The method is simple and suitable for short, steep tapers, but the feed is hand-controlled so the finish and accuracy depend on the operator, and the length of taper is limited by the compound rest travel.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Differentiate counter-sinking and counter-boring with neat sketches.
questions.solution: Counterboring produces a cylindrical, flat-bottomed recess at the top of a hole using a counterbore tool. It accommodates the cylindrical head of a socket-head cap screw so that the head sits flush or below the surface, and it can also true the end of a hole. Countersinking produces a conical recess with a countersink tool, usually at 82° or 90°, to accept the conical head of a flat-head screw or rivet. Counterboring gives a straight-walled seat; countersinking gives an angled seat.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Explain the specification of a lathe with a neat sketch.
questions.solution: A lathe is specified by: the swing over the bed (largest workpiece diameter that can rotate without hitting the bed), the swing over the cross-slide, the distance between centres (maximum workpiece length), the bed length and width, the spindle bore and spindle nose type, the spindle speed range (rpm), the feed range and lead-screw pitch, the tailstock taper, the motor power and the overall dimensions and mass. These parameters determine the largest workpiece the lathe can hold and the range of cutting conditions available.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Explain boring, counterboring, countersinking, spot facing and tapping operations.
questions.solution: Boring enlarges and trues an existing hole with a single-point tool. Counterboring cuts a flat-bottomed cylindrical recess so a socket-head screw can sit below the surface. Countersinking cuts a conical recess for a flat-head screw or rivet. Spot facing produces a flat, smooth seating surface around a hole, usually for a washer or bolt head, without enlarging the hole. Tapping cuts internal threads in a drilled hole using a tap, usually after drilling a tapping-size hole. These operations are often performed on a drilling machine, lathe or machining centre.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Describe the function of any five major parts of a lathe.
questions.solution: 1. Bed: rigid base with guideways on which the carriage and tailstock slide. 2. Headstock: houses the spindle and gearing; holds and rotates the workpiece and provides speed selection. 3. Tailstock: supports the free end of long work with a centre, and holds drills or reamers. 4. Carriage: carries the tool post and moves the cutting tool longitudinally and transversely; it includes the saddle, cross-slide, compound rest and apron. 5. Feed mechanism: lead screw, feed rod and apron gears that move the carriage or cross-slide at the selected feed for turning, threading and facing.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: A machine is being designed in which four different speeds are required. Suggest a suitable system and explain its construction and working with a neat sketch.
questions.solution: A stepped-cone pulley (speed cone) system is suitable. Each of the two shafts carries a cone with four steps of different diameters, connected by a belt. Because the belt can be moved from one pair of steps to another, four different speed ratios are obtained: N2/N1 = D1/D2. The cones are arranged in opposite directions so that the belt length remains approximately constant. The drive is simple and inexpensive, but the speeds are discrete and the belt may slip under heavy load; a geared speed box is an alternative for positive drive.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Explain draft and shrinkage allowances used in the casting process with neat sketches.
questions.solution: Draft allowance is a small taper given to the vertical faces of a pattern so that it can be withdrawn from the mould without damaging the sand. It is usually 1-3° and depends on the pattern height and the moulding method. Shrinkage allowance makes the pattern slightly larger than the finished casting to compensate for the contraction of the metal as it solidifies and cools. It depends on the material (about 1% for cast iron, 1.5-2% for steel, 1.3% for aluminium) and is added to all dimensions.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Explain the significance of the following moulding sand properties: (i) permeability, (ii) flowability, (iii) cohesiveness and (iv) refractoriness.
questions.solution: (i) Permeability is the ability of the sand to allow gases and steam to escape through the mould; low permeability causes blowholes and porosity. (ii) Flowability is the ability of the sand to flow around the pattern and fill the mould uniformly under ramming, giving a faithful impression. (iii) Cohesiveness is the ability of the sand grains to stick together so that the mould retains its shape and edges during handling and pouring. (iv) Refractoriness is the ability to withstand the high temperature of molten metal without fusing or burning, preventing sand fusion and defects.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Explain the defects in castings.
questions.solution: Common casting defects include: blowholes and porosity, caused by trapped gases; shrinkage cavities, caused by inadequate feeding during solidification; hot tears and cracks, caused by restrained contraction; misrun and cold shuts, caused by low pouring temperature or poor fluidity; sand inclusions and scabs, caused by loose or eroded mould sand; metal penetration, caused by coarse sand; warpage, caused by uneven cooling; and flash or mismatch, caused by poor pattern or mould alignment. Defects are controlled by good mould design, proper gating and risering, correct pouring temperature and sand quality.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Explain with a neat sketch the steps involved in preparing a green sand mould using the two-box method.
questions.solution: 1. Place the drag (bottom flask) on a board and set the pattern on it. 2. Sprinkle parting sand, then fill the drag with green sand and ram it uniformly. 3. Turn the drag over, place the cope on it and locate the pattern's other half. 4. Insert the sprue pin and riser pin, fill the cope with sand and ram it. 5. Vent the sand with a wire to allow gases to escape. 6. Separate the cope and drag, remove the pattern, and repair any damage. 7. Cut the gate and runner channels connecting the sprue to the mould cavity. 8. Close the mould, clamp it and pour the molten metal.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Explain single-piece and split patterns used in casting.
questions.solution: A single-piece (solid) pattern is made in one piece and is used for simple shapes that can be withdrawn from the mould in one direction. It is cheaper and easier to make but is limited to simple, shallow castings. A split pattern is made in two or more parts that fit together at the parting line. One half is moulded in the drag and the other in the cope, which allows more complex shapes to be withdrawn easily. The halves are located with dowel pins to maintain alignment. Split patterns are widely used for cylindrical and irregular castings.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Describe any five pattern-making allowances.
questions.solution: 1. Shrinkage (contraction) allowance: the pattern is made larger to compensate for metal contraction during solidification and cooling. 2. Draft allowance: a small taper on vertical faces so the pattern can be withdrawn without damaging the mould. 3. Machining allowance: extra material left on surfaces that will be machined after casting. 4. Distortion allowance: an opposite deformation is built into the pattern to compensate for warping during cooling. 5. Shake or rapping allowance: a small negative allowance to compensate for the enlargement of the mould cavity when the pattern is rapped before withdrawal. Other allowances include core-print and finish allowances.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: With a neat sketch, explain the working of resistance spot welding.
questions.solution: Two overlapping metal sheets are clamped between copper electrodes and a large current is passed for a short time. The highest resistance is at the interface between the sheets, so heat is concentrated there and a small molten nugget forms. The current is switched off and the pressure is maintained while the nugget solidifies, producing a spot weld. The heat generated is H = I²Rt. Spot welding is fast and is widely used in car bodies and sheet-metal assemblies.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Suggest a suitable welding process that uses a non-consumable electrode and facilitates joining of dissimilar metals.
questions.solution: Tungsten inert gas (TIG) welding, also called gas tungsten arc welding, is suitable. A non-consumable tungsten electrode strikes an arc with the workpiece, and an inert gas such as argon or helium shields the weld pool from oxidation. Filler metal is added separately if required. Because the heat input and filler composition can be controlled independently, TIG is well suited to dissimilar metals, thin sheets and high-quality joints.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Explain the electric arc welding process with a neat sketch.
questions.solution: An electric arc is struck between a consumable electrode and the workpiece, producing intense heat (about 3000-6000°C) that melts the base metal and the electrode tip. The molten metal from the electrode is deposited in the joint, while the electrode coating forms a slag and gas shield that protects the weld from oxidation. The power source may be AC or DC, and the electrode is moved along the joint to build the weld bead. Arc welding is versatile and widely used for structural steel work.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Differentiate between soldering and brazing.
questions.solution: Soldering uses a filler metal with a melting point below 450°C (typically a tin-lead or tin-silver alloy). The base metal does not melt; the filler is drawn into the joint by capillary action. It gives a low-strength joint, used for electrical connections and sheet-metal work. Brazing uses a filler with a melting point above 450°C (such as a copper-zinc or silver alloy). It also relies on capillary action and does not melt the base metal, but produces a stronger, higher-temperature joint used for pipes, carbide tools and dissimilar metals. Both require a flux to prevent oxidation.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: With neat sketches, explain arc welding and oxy-acetylene gas welding.
questions.solution: Arc welding: an electric arc between a consumable electrode and the workpiece melts the metal; the electrode coating provides a shielding gas and slag. The molten pool solidifies to form the weld. It is fast, produces high heat and is suitable for thick sections. Oxy-acetylene gas welding: acetylene and oxygen are mixed in a torch and burned at the tip, producing a flame with a temperature of about 3200°C. The inner cone of the flame melts the base metal and a filler rod is added. A reducing (carburizing), neutral or oxidizing flame can be selected depending on the metal. It is portable and suitable for thin sheets, pipes and repair work.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Explain the characteristics of additive manufacturing.
questions.solution: Additive manufacturing builds parts layer by layer from a digital model, rather than removing material from a blank. It needs no dedicated mould or tooling, so complex internal features, lattice structures and customized parts can be made economically in small batches. Material waste is low because only the required material is deposited. However, build rates are low, surface finish often needs post-processing, and large parts may require support structures. Common processes include FDM, SLA, SLS and SLM.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Explain the limitations of NC machines.
questions.solution: NC machines have high initial cost and require expensive maintenance and trained programmers. A part program must be prepared for every job, and changes require editing or rewriting the program. The machine cannot adapt automatically to tool wear, material variation or unexpected disturbances, so quality depends on the program and setup. Dedicated fixtures and careful planning are often needed, and the system may be uneconomical for very small or simple batches. Retrofit and software costs can also be significant.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Why is additive manufacturing called so? List the steps involved in making parts using this technique.
questions.solution: It is called additive because the part is built by adding material layer upon layer, in contrast to subtractive manufacturing, which removes material from a larger block. Steps: (1) create a 3D CAD model; (2) convert it to STL or another mesh/ sliced format; (3) slice the model into thin layers and generate tool paths; (4) set up the machine with the correct material and supports; (5) build the part layer by layer; (6) remove supports and perform post-processing such as curing, machining or surface finishing.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: What advantages do you see with the installation of CNC machines on a shop floor? List any six points.
questions.solution: 1. High accuracy and repeatability, with consistent part quality. 2. Complex profiles and contours can be machined in one setup. 3. Reduced scrap and rework. 4. Quick changeover between jobs through stored programs, making small batches economical. 5. Less dependence on operator skill and reduced fatigue. 6. Lower direct labour cost and shorter lead times. Additional benefits include better tool-life monitoring, reduced inspection, and easy implementation of CAD/CAM and unattended machining.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: With a neat sketch illustrating the pressure and velocity changes, explain the working of a reaction turbine.
questions.solution: A reaction turbine uses the reaction force produced when steam expands and accelerates through stationary and moving blades. Steam from the boiler first passes through a set of fixed (guide) blades, where it expands and its pressure falls while its velocity rises. It then enters the moving blades, where it continues to expand; the pressure drops further and the relative velocity increases, producing a reaction force on the blades in addition to the impulse from the change in direction. Because expansion occurs in both fixed and moving blades, the pressure falls progressively from stage to stage while the velocity rises and falls alternately. The moving blades are therefore of increasing height and the rotor is partly full of steam, so the turbine must be enclosed and usually has several stages. The pressure-velocity diagram shows pressure decreasing continuously across each stage and velocity rising in the fixed blades and falling in the moving blades.
questions.note: Asked for 5 marks in the 2016 paper and 10 marks in the 2019 paper.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Justify the statement: a single-stage impulse turbine is suitable only for small power generation plants.
questions.solution: In a single-stage impulse turbine the whole pressure drop takes place in one set of nozzles and the steam leaves the stage at high velocity. A large part of the kinetic energy is lost in the leaving steam, so the stage efficiency is low. The rotor also runs at a very high speed for a good velocity ratio, which limits the size and the power that can be transmitted. Since only one stage is available, the enthalpy drop per stage is limited and a large power output would require an impractically large steam flow or wheel. Multiple stages are therefore used for larger plants to extract energy progressively and improve efficiency.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: With a neat schematic diagram, explain the working principle of a thermal power plant.
questions.solution: A thermal power plant converts the chemical energy of coal into electrical energy through a steam cycle. Coal is pulverized and burned in the boiler furnace, transferring heat to water in the boiler tubes. The water evaporates and the steam is superheated, then expanded through a steam turbine, which drives an alternator to generate electricity. The exhaust steam is condensed in a condenser, usually cooled by circulating water from a cooling tower or river, and the condensate is pumped back to the boiler by the feed pump through feedwater heaters. The flue gases pass over an economizer and air preheater before being cleaned in an electrostatic precipitator and released through the chimney. The main components are the coal handling plant, boiler, superheater, turbine, generator, condenser, cooling tower and feedwater system. The cycle is the Rankine cycle, and its efficiency is improved by high steam pressure and temperature and by regenerative feed heating.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Explain with a neat sketch any one type of water turbine.
questions.solution: A Pelton wheel is an impulse water turbine used for high heads and low discharges. Water from the reservoir is carried through a penstock to one or more nozzles. Each nozzle converts the pressure energy of the water into kinetic energy, producing a high-velocity jet that strikes the buckets on the runner. The buckets are double-cup shaped with a central splitter, so the jet is divided into two halves and turned through nearly 180°, giving a large change in momentum and hence a large impulse. The runner rotates and drives a generator through a shaft. A spear valve inside the nozzle regulates the flow, and a deflector plate is used to divert the jet during load rejection. The casing is not water-tight; it only prevents splashing. Pelton wheels are suitable for heads above about 100 m.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Explain the working principle of an impulse, tangential-flow water turbine.
questions.solution: The Pelton wheel is the common impulse, tangential-flow water turbine. A high-velocity jet from a nozzle strikes the buckets tangentially at the pitch circle of the runner. The jet is split by the bucket's central ridge, flows over the two cup-shaped halves and leaves with a small absolute velocity in the opposite direction. The change in the tangential momentum of the water produces an impulse on each bucket, and the resulting torque rotates the runner. Because the jet strikes only part of the runner at a time and the pressure all around the runner is atmospheric, the casing is not pressure-tight. The turbine is used for high heads and low flows, and the nozzle area is adjusted with a spear to control the flow and power.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Briefly explain with a sketch the working principle of a gas turbine.
questions.solution: A gas turbine works on the Brayton cycle. Air is compressed in a compressor, fuel is burned with the compressed air in a combustion chamber at essentially constant pressure, and the high-temperature, high-pressure gases expand through a turbine. The turbine drives the compressor, and the remaining power drives a generator or a propeller through a shaft; in an open-cycle plant the exhaust gases are discharged to atmosphere. The main components are the compressor, combustion chamber and turbine, and the machine is compact and quick-starting but needs clean fuel and has lower part-load efficiency.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Draw the schematic diagrams of nuclear and thermal power plants.
questions.solution: Thermal plant: coal handling -> boiler furnace -> superheater -> steam turbine -> generator; turbine exhaust -> condenser -> feed pump -> economizer/feedwater heaters -> boiler; flue gases -> economizer -> air preheater -> electrostatic precipitator -> chimney; condenser cooling water -> cooling tower. Nuclear plant: reactor core (fuel rods, moderator, control rods, coolant) -> heat exchanger/steam generator -> steam turbine -> generator; turbine exhaust -> condenser -> feed pump -> steam generator; the primary coolant circulates in a closed loop between the reactor and the steam generator, and a concrete biological shield surrounds the reactor. In a boiling-water reactor the steam is raised directly in the reactor and goes to the turbine, while in a pressurized-water reactor the primary loop heats a secondary loop in the steam generator.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Explain the functions of an evaporator and a compressor in a vapour compression refrigeration system.
questions.solution: The evaporator is the low-pressure heat exchanger where the refrigerant boils at a low temperature, absorbing heat from the space to be cooled; this produces the refrigerating effect. The compressor draws low-pressure vapour from the evaporator, compresses it to a higher pressure and temperature, and delivers it to the condenser. The compressor is the heart of the system: it maintains the pressure difference between the evaporator and condenser and circulates the refrigerant.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Explain the essential properties required for a good refrigerant.
questions.solution: A good refrigerant should have a high latent heat of vaporization and a high critical temperature, so a small mass can produce a large refrigerating effect. It should have a low boiling point, be non-toxic, non-flammable, non-corrosive, chemically stable and miscible with lubricating oil. It should be easily detectable if it leaks, have a low cost, and operate with evaporator and condenser pressures that are modest and preferably above atmospheric to prevent air ingress. It should also have a low specific volume to keep the compressor size small.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Justify the statement: an ideal refrigerant should have a high latent heat of evaporation, and the evaporator and condenser pressures should be above atmospheric pressure.
questions.solution: A high latent heat means a smaller mass flow of refrigerant is needed for a given refrigerating effect, so the compressor and piping can be smaller and the power consumption is lower. Pressures above atmospheric prevent air and moisture from leaking into the system, which would reduce performance and cause corrosion or freezing at the expansion valve. The pressures should still be moderate to avoid excessively strong components.

questions.subject: basic-mechanical
questions.question: Describe the function of (i) the evaporator, (ii) the compressor or circulating system, (iii) the condenser and (iv) the expansion valve in a vapour compression refrigeration system.
questions.solution: (i) Evaporator: low-pressure refrigerant liquid evaporates by absorbing heat from the refrigerated space, producing the cooling effect. (ii) Compressor: draws low-pressure vapour, compresses it to condenser pressure and temperature, and circulates the refrigerant through the circuit. (iii) Condenser: rejects heat from the high-pressure vapour to the surroundings, condensing it back to liquid. (iv) Expansion valve: throttles the high-pressure liquid to the low evaporator pressure, causing partial flashing and a temperature drop before the refrigerant enters the evaporator. The cycle then repeats.
